title: How to keep things organized/modular to reserve tokens?
author: Accurate-Bear7198
selftext:
Hey guys, I'm just wondering if any of you have figured out the best workflow/file structures for building a game so the ai knows how to get to things really fast and easily when you ask for changes or improvements, instead of grepping and searching for ages and using all those credits and having to index large files over and over?

I'm using godot with mcp server right now, that seems to help a bit, but still takes a while just to land on what it needs and ends up using a lot of tokens for very simple changes like changing the camera angle for characters or swapping out sound files

comments.author: fhtiek
comments.body:
Couple things you can do:

-Have it build out project markdown files as you work that detail where stuff is and provides succinct descriptions of things. This is something you tell it to bake into your work, new features or entities get their own markdown files. Reading one of these is a lot less token intensive then using the mcp to look for things directly in the project and lets the agent go right to the source rather than searching and looping.

-Stop having it do things you can easily do yourself. You can burn a lot of tokens fine tuning things when you will work faster and more efficiently if you instead have it expose constants for you to tune yourself. I found myself saying things like "make the slide 200ms longer" "reduce lantern brightness by 10 percent" and "make aggro range 5ft shorter". This is crazy inefficient. Its better to have it design features so that there are exposed constants and/or gui controls you can use to do this fine tuning yourself. Your example of moving the camera angle is a good one, thats really simple if your object hierarchy is set up conveniently, so do those changes yourself, its probably faster anyways than waiting for it to think.

replies.author: Accurate-Bear7198
replies.body: Thats actually a great point, i found myself doing that as well and it would take like 5 minutes just to tune a knob...

comments.author: InformationTop5376
comments.body:
What I’ve done is create markdown files with explicit instruction for my Claude opus 5.5 session to spin off sonnet sessions if it deems the task is sonnet-worthy. (You could do the same thing with Astra/Sol I suppose).

Another thing I do since I use GitHub Pull Requests to coordinate my work across different sessions, is to have the AI create scripts that use common CLI commands so it doesn’t have to reach into its token pool to figure that out. It has a reference to each script and what it does. This might be a wash but not sure.

But definitely seeing a bit of a difference on the sonnet subagent workflow.

comments.author: fhtiek
comments.body:
If youre not, I also recommend using github for a repo. I have a main .md folder where a succinct map of the whole project lives in a contents.md file. Contents.md points to other more detailed .md files for specific features, entities, workflows, etc. My token churn went way down doing this and baking in instruction to find the needed info there first. Otherwise it starts opening and analyzing 3D models, or searching the internet for info it already posseses. 

Just one word of caution, instruct your agent not to run github actions unless you tell it to. Github bills for actions above a threshold unless your reponis public. I got it up to a $12 invoice before i realized necause the agent was running the actions on every change

comments.author: Robonotes1760
comments.body: Get the AI to create an interlinked knowledge based of markdown documents summarising your code and critical architectural and design decisions.

comments.author: 3tt07kjt
comments.body:
Let’s say I ask for something *supposed* to be simple, like “make the camera angle wider when running”, and it spends a long time. Here’s what I do:

* I ask “why did that take so long, I thought it would be simple?”
* I look at the affected code & diffs
* I write down followup tasks to make the process faster (well, I have AI write it down)

The problem is that there are so many different ways your project could be organized bad and eat up tokens. Sometimes it's a problem with modularity (code to affect one thing is spread across too many files), a problem with fragile tests (tests break when they shouldn’t), or a problem with large markdown files eating your tokens (maybe you commit a 20-line markdown file with some design decisions, and then come back a week later and it’s 5,000 lines, eating tokens every time the AI reads it).

Basic stuff like swapping out sound files—I can do that myself. Likewise, camera angle. For sound files, I am definitely spending time listening to each file before I put it in my game, so it is going to take time regardless. Camera angle should be a slider in the editor (unless you want it controlled by code).

comments.author: DreamBigGamesReddit
comments.body:
Maybe this is dumb, but I literally spelled it out for chat the other day:

“I am broke and cannot afford to keep re-upping on tokens when 5 hour usage runs out. Optimize our work flow to maximize returns for the current usage, and try to keep usage low whenever possible. Let me know before you perform actions that will require a lot of tokens so we can decide if it’s the best use of the current usage limits”

After I said that, my prompts got a lot more efficient and it started creating more efficient prompts for codex that required much less usage and re-prompting to fix issues.

comments.author: Fuzzzy420
comments.body:
Yeah I think I have, after failing on exactly that a couple of times. 
A file size limit of 300 lines
B headers with explanations to each file
C folders don't really matter to ai
D explain to the ai ahead of time what the plan is and make a good structure part of the planning
E ai will always search but how long is the question 
F have a good roadmap with one master plan that plans for deligation and multi tasking


Im working on a tool that allows ai to find any line of code through context search with one or two mcp calls and no searching. But it takes forever.
